gloss: A dirty or untidy state of a place or thing.
examples: The kitchen was a *mess* after the party.
Clean up your *mess* before you go out.
The kids make three *messes* a day.

gloss: The work of clearing away dirt or damage after an event.
examples: The *cleanup* took longer than the party itself.
Volunteers showed up for the river *cleanup*.
After the storm there were *cleanups* going on all over town.
contrast: The noun is one word, *cleanup*; the verb is two, *clean up*.

gloss: A lot of small things lying around where they do not belong.
examples: The counter disappeared under all the *clutter*.
She spent Sunday getting rid of *clutter*.
There's too much *clutter* in this room.
contrast: Uncountable: *a lot of clutter*, never *a clutter* or *clutters*.

gloss: Old things that have no value and should be thrown away.
examples: The garage is full of *junk*.
He hauled a truckload of *junk* to the dump.
Most of what she kept was *junk*.
contrast: Uncountable: *a piece of junk*, never *a junk*.

gloss: A container you drop everyday waste into.
examples: Throw that in the *trash can*.
The *trash can* by the door is full again.
There are *trash cans* every fifty feet along the boardwalk.
contrast: American *trash can*; the British say *bin* or *dustbin*.

gloss: A large container for household waste, often kept outside.
examples: Roll the *garbage can* out to the curb tonight.
A raccoon knocked over the *garbage can* again.
The *garbage cans* are behind the fence.

gloss: A plastic bag used to line a can and carry waste out.
examples: Grab a *trash bag* from under the sink.
The *trash bag* split on the way down the stairs.
We went through six *trash bags* cleaning the basement.

gloss: A sheet of absorbent paper torn off a roll to wipe up spills.
examples: Hand me a *paper towel* — I spilled the coffee.
We're out of *paper towels* again.
She wiped the counter with a damp *paper towel*.
contrast: American *paper towels*; the British call the roll *kitchen roll*.

gloss: A machine that sucks dust and dirt off floors and carpets.
examples: The *vacuum cleaner* is in the hall closet.
Our old *vacuum cleaner* finally died.
They sell *vacuum cleaners* on the second floor.
contrast: *Vacuum* is spelled with two u's — one of the few English words that is.

gloss: The soap-like liquid or powder used for washing clothes.
examples: Pick up some *laundry detergent* while you're out.
She uses the unscented *laundry detergent*.
A bottle of *laundry detergent* lasts us a month.
contrast: Uncountable: *a bottle of laundry detergent*, not *a laundry detergent*.

gloss: Liquid soap made for washing dishes by hand.
examples: Add a squirt of *dish soap* to the water.
We're almost out of *dish soap*.
*Dish soap* works fine for handwashing sweaters.
contrast: American *dish soap*; the British say *washing-up liquid*.

gloss: A cloth towel used to dry dishes and hands in the kitchen.
examples: Dry that pan with a *dish towel*.
The *dish towel* is hanging on the oven handle.
She keeps clean *dish towels* in the top drawer.
contrast: American *dish towel*; the British say *tea towel*.

gloss: A small cloth used to wash dishes and wipe counters.
examples: Wring out the *dishcloth* and hang it up.
That *dishcloth* smells — throw it in the wash.
She knits her own *dishcloths*.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A liquid or powder made for cleaning a particular surface.

This *cleaner* is safe on granite.
The store carries a dozen different bathroom *cleaners*.
contrast: *Cleaner* is also the person who cleans: *the cleaner comes Fridays*.

gloss: A damp disposable cloth sold in a pack for quick cleaning.
examples: Keep a pack of *wipes* in the car.
She pulled a *wipe* out and cleaned his hands.
Disinfecting *wipes* sold out in a week.
contrast: Almost always plural — you buy *wipes*, not *a wipe*.

gloss: A quick wash in clean water to take soap or dirt off.
examples: Give the plate a *rinse* before it goes in the dishwasher.
One more *rinse* and the suds will be gone.
The machine runs two *rinses* on that setting.

gloss: A period of leaving something in water so dirt loosens.
examples: That pan needs a long *soak*.
Give the shirt an overnight *soak* in cold water.
A couple of *soaks* got most of the grease out.

gloss: The bubbles that form on water when soap is added.
examples: The sink was full of *suds*.
Rinse it until there are no *suds* left.
*Suds* were coming out from under the washer.

gloss: The thick white foam soap makes when you rub it with water.

Work up a good *lather* before you scrub.

gloss: A hard rubbing with a brush or cloth to get dirt off.
examples: The tub needs a good *scrub*.
Give that baking sheet a serious *scrub*.
Two *scrubs* with baking soda and the stain was gone.

gloss: One cleaning of something with water, or the clothes being washed.
examples: My jeans are in the *wash*.
The car could use a *wash*.
The color faded after three *washes*.

gloss: An open basket for carrying clothes to and from the washer.
examples: Carry the *laundry basket* downstairs for me.
The clean towels are still in the *laundry basket*.
We keep two *laundry baskets* in the closet.

gloss: The room in a house or building where clothes are washed.
examples: The washer and dryer are in the *laundry room*.
Our building has a *laundry room* in the basement.
Newer apartments here have their own *laundry rooms*.

gloss: A thin scented sheet put in the dryer to soften clothes.

I can smell the *dryer sheet* from the hallway.
*Dryer sheets* leave a film on the lint trap.

gloss: A liquid added to the rinse to make clothes feel softer.

The whole basement smells like *fabric softener*.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A product sprayed or rubbed on a mark to lift it out of cloth.

This *stain remover* actually works on red wine.
None of the *stain removers* touched the ink.

gloss: A padded folding table you press clothes on.
examples: Set up the *ironing board* by the window.
The *ironing board* lives behind the door.
Hotel rooms usually have *ironing boards* in the closet.
contrast: *Iron* is said EYE-urn — the r comes before the n, not after.

gloss: A shop that cleans clothes with chemicals instead of water.
examples: My suit is at the *dry cleaner*.
There's a *dry cleaner* two doors down from the bank.

contrast: Americans say both *at the dry cleaner* and *at the dry cleaner's*.

gloss: The process of cleaning clothes with a chemical solvent.
examples: This coat needs *dry cleaning*.
*Dry cleaning* costs more every year.
Can you pick up the *dry cleaning* on your way home?

gloss: One complete run of a washing machine from filling to draining.
examples: The *wash cycle* takes about fifty minutes.
Use the gentle *wash cycle* for that sweater.
The machine has eight *wash cycles* and I use two.

gloss: The part of the wash when the drum spins fast to squeeze out water.
examples: The whole house shakes during the *spin cycle*.
Skip the *spin cycle* on anything with lace.
Slow *spin cycles* are gentler on knits.

gloss: The white clothes and sheets washed together in one load.

The *whites* go in on hot.

gloss: Thin or fragile clothes that need a gentle wash.

There's a separate setting for *delicates*.
She washes her *delicates* by hand.

gloss: A sticky roller on a handle for pulling fuzz and hair off clothes.
examples: Run a *lint roller* over that jacket.
I keep a *lint roller* in my desk because of the cat.

gloss: The screen in a dryer that catches fuzz from the clothes.

gloss: A folding frame you hang wet clothes on to dry indoors.

Set up the *drying rack* by the radiator.
The *drying racks* take up half the balcony.

gloss: A long zippered bag that protects a suit or dress on a hanger.
examples: The dress came back from the cleaner in a *garment bag*.
Hang the tux in a *garment bag* so it doesn't wrinkle.
Two *garment bags* barely fit in the trunk.

gloss: A cloth or mesh bag for carrying or protecting dirty clothes.

Wash the bras in a mesh *laundry bag*.
Students show up with *laundry bags* every Sunday.

gloss: A shaft in a house that drops dirty clothes to the floor below.

The old house has a *laundry chute* in the hallway.
Builders stopped putting in *laundry chutes* years ago.

gloss: Clothes and sheets that are waiting to be washed.
examples: There's a week of *dirty laundry* on his floor.

gloss: The way dried clothes stick to each other or to the body.
examples: That skirt has terrible *static cling* in winter.
A dryer sheet cuts down on *static cling*.
*Static cling* is worse when the air is dry.

gloss: An iron that pushes hot vapor through cloth to smooth it.
examples: Fill the *steam iron* with distilled water.
A *steam iron* takes the creases right out.
They had three *steam irons* in the back room.
contrast: *Iron* sounds like EYE-urn — the r is said before the n.

gloss: A handheld device that smooths clothes with hot vapor.
examples: Run the *steamer* over that jacket before you wear it.
A *steamer* is faster than ironing for curtains.
The shop keeps two *steamers* by the fitting rooms.

gloss: A washer or dryer setting that keeps clothes from wrinkling.
examples: Dry the shirts on *permanent press*.
*Permanent press* uses a cooler tumble.
Put the work pants on *permanent press* and they come out flat.

gloss: Dirt that has built up on a surface and is hard to remove.
examples: Years of *grime* covered the windows.
Hot water and soap cut through the *grime*.
The stove was black with *grime*.
contrast: Uncountable — never *a grime* or *grimes*.

gloss: Disgusting dirt, especially where people live.

Inspectors found *filth* in the kitchen.
They lived in *filth* for months.
contrast: Uncountable — *filth*, never *filths*.

gloss: Loose broken pieces left lying around after damage or use.

There was *debris* all over the yard after the storm.

gloss: A thin gray or white growth that forms on damp surfaces.
examples: There's *mildew* along the bottom of the shower curtain.
Wet towels in a pile will grow *mildew*.
Bleach kills *mildew* on tile.
contrast: Uncountable — never *a mildew*.

gloss: A dirty film that forms on the top of water or on a wet surface.
examples: There was *scum* floating on the dishwater.
Wipe the *scum* off the waterline of the tub.
Green *scum* covered the top of the barrel.

gloss: The chalky film soap leaves on tile, glass, and tubs.
examples: The shower door is covered in *soap scum*.
Vinegar takes off *soap scum*.

gloss: A layer of dirt or residue that has collected slowly over time.
examples: There's a *buildup* of grease behind the stove.
The showerhead had a mineral *buildup*.
Regular cleaning prevents *buildups* like that.

gloss: Thick wet dirt, especially mud mixed with waste.
examples: His boots were caked with *muck*.
They shoveled the *muck* out of the barn.
Rain turned the path into *muck*.

gloss: Sticky, greasy dirt of no particular kind.
examples: There's *gunk* stuck in the drain.
He scraped the *gunk* off the burner.
The filter was full of black *gunk*.

gloss: Thick, soft mud or waste that settles at the bottom.
examples: Black *sludge* came out of the pipe.
There was *sludge* in the bottom of the tank.
The plant treats *sludge* before it's hauled away.

gloss: A wet slippery layer, often greenish, on a damp surface.
examples: The birdbath was coated in *slime*.
Scrub the *slime* off the steps before someone slips.
There's *slime* growing in the drain.

gloss: Dried-on dirt or food stuck to a surface.
examples: There's *crud* baked onto the pan.
He chipped the *crud* off the grill.
Get the *crud* out of the corners with a toothbrush.

gloss: A sticky, wet substance that is hard to wipe off.
examples: Some kind of *goo* leaked in the fridge.
The sticker left *goo* on the glass.
Rubbing alcohol takes that *goo* right off.

gloss: Tiny hard bits of sand or dirt you can feel underfoot.
examples: There's *grit* all over the kitchen floor.
Rinse the *grit* out of the lettuce.
You could feel the *grit* between your teeth.

gloss: A dirty mark made by rubbing something wet or greasy.
examples: There's a *smear* of jam on the counter.
The window was full of *smears* after he wiped it.
A *smear* of grease ran down the cabinet door.

gloss: A mark made by liquid flying out and landing in drops.
examples: Wipe the grease *splatter* off the backsplash.
There were paint *splatters* all over the drop cloth.
A tomato sauce *splatter* dried on the microwave door.

gloss: A large irregular mark of color or dirt.
examples: A dark *blotch* spread across the ceiling.
The bleach left pale *blotches* on the shirt.
There's a *blotch* on the carpet by the door.

gloss: A messy, uneven spot of liquid or dirt.
examples: There's a *splotch* of oil on the driveway.
Coffee left a brown *splotch* on the report.
*Splotches* of mildew showed along the grout.
contrast: *Splotch* and *blotch* mean nearly the same thing; both are common.

gloss: A very small spot or piece of something on a surface.
examples: There were *flecks* of paint on the floor.
A *fleck* of dried egg was stuck to the fork.
Brush the *flecks* of lint off your collar.

gloss: A patch where something has lost or changed its color.
examples: Bleach left a yellow *discoloration* on the towel.
There's some *discoloration* under the sink from the leak.
Small *discolorations* showed where the sun hit the couch.
contrast: American *discoloration*; the British spell it *discolouration*.

gloss: The dull dark film that forms on silver and other metals.
examples: The candlesticks were covered in *tarnish*.
This polish takes *tarnish* off in seconds.
You can see the *tarnish* around the handle.

gloss: A soft ball of dust and hair that collects under furniture.
examples: A *dust bunny* rolled out from under the bed.
There are *dust bunnies* behind the dresser.
The vacuum got every *dust bunny* in the hall.

gloss: An old soft cloth kept for wiping dust off surfaces.
examples: Grab a *dust rag* and do the shelves.
She tore up an old T-shirt for *dust rags*.
The *dust rag* was gray by the time she finished.

gloss: A smell, usually an unpleasant one.
examples: A strange *odor* was coming from the fridge.
The spray is supposed to neutralize *odors*.
There's a faint *odor* of smoke in the hallway.
contrast: American spelling *odor*; British *odour*.

gloss: Something you notice with your nose, good or bad.
examples: What's that *smell* in the basement?
The *smell* of bleach filled the bathroom.
Cooking *smells* stay in the curtains.

gloss: A strong bad smell.
examples: The *stink* from the trash can hit us at the door.
It took two days for the *stink* to go away.
There was an awful *stink* under the porch.

gloss: A very strong, disgusting smell.
examples: The *stench* of rotting garbage filled the alley.
You could smell the *stench* from the street.
Nothing covered up the *stench*.

gloss: A short, faint smell you catch for a moment.
examples: I caught a *whiff* of ammonia.
There was a *whiff* of mildew in the closet.
Every so often you get *whiffs* of something burning.

gloss: The clean, pleasant quality of air or laundry that smells new.
examples: The label promises thirty days of *freshness*.
There's a *freshness* to sheets dried outside.
Open a window for a little *freshness*.

gloss: A spray or plug-in that puts a pleasant scent into a room.
examples: There's an *air freshener* plugged in by the door.
The *air freshener* just covers up the smell.
Those pine *air fresheners* hang from every mirror.

gloss: A product that removes a bad smell instead of masking it.
examples: Sprinkle carpet *deodorizer* before you vacuum.
Baking soda works as a *deodorizer* in the fridge.
They tried three *deodorizers* on the smoke smell.

gloss: The absorbent part of a mop that touches the floor.
examples: The *mop head* needs replacing.
Wring the *mop head* out over the bucket.
Extra *mop heads* are on the bottom shelf.

gloss: A flat mop used dry to pick dust off hard floors.
examples: Run the *dust mop* over the hardwood first.
A *dust mop* gets under the couch better than a broom.
The school buys *dust mops* by the case.

gloss: A broom with a wide head, used for sweeping large floors.
examples: He cleared the garage with a *push broom*.
Grab the *push broom* out of the shed.
Two *push brooms* leaned against the wall.

gloss: A stiff-bristled brush for rubbing dirt off hard surfaces.
examples: Take a *scrub brush* to that grout.
The *scrub brush* is under the sink.
We went through two *scrub brushes* on the deck.
contrast: American *scrub brush*; the British say *scrubbing brush*.

gloss: A rough pad or tool used to rub stuck-on dirt away.
examples: Use the blue *scrubber* on the pan, not the sponge.
That *scrubber* will scratch the nonstick coating.
A pack of *scrubbers* costs two dollars.

gloss: A rough pad used to scrape burned or dried food off cookware.
examples: Hit the casserole dish with a *scouring pad*.
A *scouring pad* will ruin that finish.
The *scouring pads* are in the drawer by the stove.

gloss: A pad of fine metal threads used for scouring and sanding.
examples: Rub the rust off with *steel wool*.
*Steel wool* leaves tiny scratches on stainless.
He stuffed *steel wool* in the hole to keep mice out.
contrast: Uncountable: *a pad of steel wool*, never *a steel wool*.

gloss: A tool with a rubber blade for pulling water off glass.
examples: Use the *squeegee* on the shower door after every shower.
There's a *squeegee* in a bucket at every gas pump.
Window washers carry three different *squeegees*.

gloss: A cloth or fluffy tool used to sweep dust off surfaces.
examples: Run a *duster* over the blinds.
The *duster* is hanging in the closet.
These *dusters* pick up more than a rag does.

gloss: A handle tipped with soft feathers for dusting delicate things.
examples: She went over the shelves with a *feather duster*.
A *feather duster* just moves the dust around.
The gift shop sold ostrich *feather dusters*.

gloss: A soft leather cloth used to dry glass and car paint without streaks.

He kept a damp *chamois* in a bucket.
Good *chamois* cost more than a pack of towels.

gloss: A round open container with a handle for carrying water.
examples: She filled a *pail* with hot soapy water.
The *pail* is out on the back steps.
Two *pails* of water later the floor was clean.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *pale*.

gloss: A waterproof glove worn to protect the hands while cleaning.
examples: Put on a *rubber glove* before you reach in there.
Wear *rubber gloves* with that cleaner.
One *rubber glove* had a hole in the thumb.

gloss: A bottle with a trigger that pushes liquid out in a fine mist.
examples: Mix vinegar and water in a *spray bottle*.
The *spray bottle* clogged after a week.
She labels her *spray bottles* with masking tape.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A liquid product that is pushed out of a container in a mist.
examples: Give the counter a quick shot of *spray*.
This *spray* takes grease off the stovetop.
The shelf was full of cleaning *sprays*.

gloss: A pressurized can that releases its contents as a fine mist.
examples: Don't throw an *aerosol* in the fire.
The polish comes in an *aerosol*.
Some *aerosols* are banned in this state.

gloss: A long-handled brush used only for cleaning inside a toilet.
examples: The *toilet brush* sits in a holder behind the tank.
Replace the *toilet brush* every few months.
Each bathroom has its own *toilet brush*.

gloss: One of the short stiff hairs or wires on a brush.
examples: The *bristles* on this brush are too soft.
A *bristle* broke off and stuck in the grout.

contrast: The t is silent: BRIS-uhl, like *whistle*.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

His office is barely bigger than a *broom closet*.
Both *broom closets* were padlocked.

gloss: A small room holding the washer, water heater, and cleaning supplies.
examples: The mop bucket is out in the *utility room*.
There's a sink in the *utility room*.
Newer houses put the *utility rooms* off the garage.

gloss: A kitchen drawer where small odd items pile up.
examples: The batteries are in the *junk drawer*.
I cleaned out the *junk drawer* and found four takeout menus.
Every house has at least two *junk drawers*.
contrast: *Drawer* is one syllable in American speech: DRAWR.

gloss: A kitchen appliance that crushes garbage into a small block.
examples: The old kitchen still has a *trash compactor*.
The *trash compactor* jammed on a soup can.
Nobody installs *trash compactors* anymore.

gloss: A grinder under the kitchen sink that chops up food waste.
examples: Don't put coffee grounds down the *garbage disposal*.
The *garbage disposal* is making an awful noise.
*Garbage disposals* are standard in apartments here.
contrast: American *garbage disposal*; the British say *waste disposal unit*.

gloss: The practice of turning used materials into new products.
examples: The town started curbside *recycling* last year.
*Recycling* goes out on Thursdays.
Glass *recycling* costs the city money.
contrast: Uncountable — never *a recycling*.

gloss: The container, usually blue, for paper, cans, and bottles.
examples: Cardboard goes in the *recycling bin*.
The *recycling bin* blew over in the wind.
There are *recycling bins* on every floor.

gloss: Materials that can be processed and used again.
examples: Rinse the *recyclables* before you put them out.
The *recyclables* go in the blue bin.
They pick up *recyclables* every other Tuesday.
contrast: Used in the plural: *the recyclables*.

gloss: A place where used materials are dropped off and sorted.
examples: Take the electronics to the *recycling center*.
The *recycling center* is open Saturday mornings.
Two *recycling centers* closed when the market dried up.
contrast: American *center*; the British spell it *centre*.

gloss: A large site where waste is buried under earth.
examples: Most of that plastic ends up in a *landfill*.
The county *landfill* closes at four.
Old *landfills* still leak into the groundwater.

gloss: A place where people leave trash and unwanted things.
examples: He took the old couch to the *dump*.
The *dump* charges by the pound now.
There used to be *dumps* at the edge of every town.

gloss: A lot where wrecked cars and scrap metal are kept.
examples: He found the part at a *junkyard*.
A dog barked behind the *junkyard* fence.
The *junkyards* out on Route 9 buy scrap by the ton.

gloss: A furnace built to burn waste.
examples: The hospital burns its waste in an *incinerator*.
Neighbors fought the new *incinerator* for years.
Old apartment buildings had *incinerators* in the basement.

gloss: Waste water and human waste carried away in pipes.
examples: Heavy rain pushed *sewage* into the river.
The plant treats *sewage* for the whole county.
There was raw *sewage* in the basement.
contrast: SOO-ij, not to be confused with *sewing* (SOH-ing).

gloss: The act of getting rid of waste properly.
examples: The city handles *disposal* of household waste.
Proper *disposal* of paint means a special drop-off.
*Disposal* of the old mattress cost forty dollars.

gloss: The truck that collects household waste from the curb.
examples: The *garbage truck* wakes us up at six.
He missed the *garbage truck* by five minutes.
Two *garbage trucks* work this route.

gloss: The day of the week when waste is collected on a street.
examples: Tomorrow is *trash day*, so put the cans out.
*Trash day* moves to Wednesday on holiday weeks.
We have two *trash days* in the summer.

gloss: A shaft in a building that carries garbage down to a bin.
examples: The *trash chute* is at the end of the hall.
Something's stuck in the *trash chute* again.
The *trash chutes* are locked after ten at night.
contrast: *Chute* sounds like *shoot*.

gloss: Someone who drops trash in a public place.
examples: Don't be a *litterbug* — there's a can right there.
The sign calls out *litterbugs* with a two-hundred-dollar fine.
A few *litterbugs* ruin the whole beach.

gloss: Waste material; in British English, what Americans call trash.
examples: Put the *rubbish* out by the gate.
The yard was full of *rubbish* and broken glass.
He said the whole story was *rubbish*.
contrast: Mainly British for trash; Americans use it to mean *nonsense*.

gloss: The systems that keep a place clean and remove waste.
examples: The strike shut down city *sanitation* for a week.
Poor *sanitation* spreads disease fast.
*Sanitation* crews start at five in the morning.

gloss: A person employed by a city to collect and handle waste.
examples: A *sanitation worker* waved at the kids from the truck.
*Sanitation workers* got a new contract in June.
His father was a *sanitation worker* for thirty years.

gloss: Someone whose job is picking up household waste.
examples: The *garbage collector* left a note on the can.
*Garbage collectors* don't take yard waste.
He worked as a *garbage collector* right out of high school.

gloss: A person who cleans and takes care of a building.
examples: The *custodian* unlocked the gym for us.
Ask the *custodian* for a mop.
The school kept two *custodians* on the night shift.

gloss: A woman employed to clean rooms in a house or hotel.
examples: The *maid* comes in to make up the room around ten.
They hired a *maid* twice a month.
The hotel *maids* were pushing carts down the hall.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *made*.

gloss: A person paid to clean and run a household.
examples: Their *housekeeper* comes on Tuesdays.
The *housekeeper* left a note about the laundry.
The hotel has *housekeepers* on every floor.

gloss: A woman hired to clean a home or office.
examples: The *cleaning lady* comes every other Friday.
We leave the key under the mat for the *cleaning lady*.
The building hires *cleaning ladies* through an agency.

gloss: A company you pay to send people to clean your home or office.
examples: We use a *cleaning service* once a month.
The *cleaning service* brings its own supplies.
She called three *cleaning services* for quotes.

gloss: The products and tools kept on hand for cleaning.
examples: The *cleaning supplies* are under the sink.
We're out of *cleaning supplies* again.
She keeps all her *cleaning supplies* in one bucket.
contrast: Used in the plural: *cleaning supplies*, not *a cleaning supply*.

gloss: The work of cleaning a home from top to bottom.
examples: Saturday is for *housecleaning*.
*Housecleaning* takes her most of the day.
He does the *housecleaning* and she cooks.
contrast: Written as one word; the verb phrase is *clean house*.

gloss: A thorough cleaning of a whole house, done once a year.
examples: We're doing *spring cleaning* this weekend.
*Spring cleaning* means the windows too.
She got through half the *spring cleaning* before it rained.

gloss: The state of being clean, or the habit of keeping things clean.
examples: The inspector praised the kitchen's *cleanliness*.
*Cleanliness* matters more than decoration in a rental.
He's fussy about *cleanliness* in the shop.
contrast: Said KLEN-lee-nuhs, with a short e — not KLEEN-.

gloss: The quality of being tidy and well arranged.
examples: Her desk is a model of *neatness*.
They grade on *neatness* as well as spelling.
There's a *neatness* to the way he folds everything.

gloss: The habit of keeping everything in its place.
examples: His *tidiness* drives his roommate crazy.
The apartment was spotless, but the *tidiness* felt cold.
*Tidiness* is the first thing she looks for in a sublet.

gloss: Extreme dirt and neglect in the place where someone lives.
examples: The family was living in *squalor*.
Inspectors found *squalor* in half the units.
He wrote about the *squalor* of the old tenements.
